author: BrentDesk Staff
headline: Saudi trade shows now open at four in the afternoon and close at ten
deck: Evening hours are becoming standard at Saudi exhibitions, and they say something about who the organisers expect to attend.
excerpt: Both the Riyadh hospitality cluster and the Jeddah building shows run 16:00 to 22:00, an evening format increasingly standard at Saudi exhibitions.
content:
Two of the larger Saudi exhibitions opening on 15 September run identical hours: the hospitality cluster at Riyadh's convention centre and JIBEX with Mobedex in Jeddah both operate from 16:00 to 22:00. Saudi Food Manufacturing in Jeddah later in the month runs 13:00 to 20:00. The Saudi Facility Management Association's Riyadh forum, by contrast, runs 09:00 to 19:00.

The split is not arbitrary and it is a useful signal about intended audience.

An exhibition running during the working day expects visitors sent by an employer — technical staff, procurement teams, engineers attending as part of their job, with travel and time approved. That is the profile of a corporate or institutional event, and it is what the FM forum's daytime hours indicate.

An exhibition running into the evening expects visitors attending on their own time. That means business owners, small contractors, independent specifiers and buyers for whom the show is a commercial opportunity rather than an assignment. It also means visitors who have worked a full day elsewhere and are attending afterwards, which changes how long they stay and what they are prepared to do while there.

For exhibitors the difference is material. An evening show concentrates traffic into a shorter, denser window, which suits products that can be demonstrated quickly and decisions that can be taken by one person. A daytime show spreads traffic across more hours with fewer visitors at any moment, which suits technical selling that requires a longer conversation.

The evening format also reflects Saudi commercial rhythms more generally. Retail and food service operate late, family activity concentrates in the evening, and an exhibition competing for discretionary attention does better after dark than at eleven in the morning. In summer months the practical case is stronger still.

There is a consequence for coverage worth noting. An event that opens at four and closes at ten compresses the window in which announcements can be made and reported, and it pushes any press activity into a part of the day when fewer outlets are working. Shows serious about generating news tend to schedule openings and conference sessions earlier regardless of when the floor opens — which the Riyadh hospitality cluster does through its summit programme, and which JIBEX, having no conference at all, does not.

Opening hours are taken from the organisers' published material. An organiser choosing evening hours is choosing an audience, and exhibitors should price their stand time accordingly. The compressed window also concentrates stand traffic, which suits exhibitors selling a product that demonstrates quickly and disadvantages those needing a long technical conversation with a buyer who arrived after a full working day elsewhere.
